title: Boundaries are kind
description: A clear boundary is not a wall against people; it is the fence that lets the garden — and the visiting — survive.

body.heading: Unstated boundaries become resentments
paragraphs: The pattern is painfully regular: a boundary is crossed silently, resentment accumulates interest, and the eventual explosion baffles the person who never knew the line existed. Most “sudden” relationship breakdowns are just long-unspoken boundaries presenting their final invoice.
Stating the line early, while you can still say it warmly, is not confrontation. It is maintenance — the cheapest kind.

body.heading: Say the boundary as information
paragraphs: A boundary lands best as information about yourself, not a verdict on them: “I don’t answer work messages after eight” rather than “You always message too late.” The first can be respected without anyone being accused of anything.
Expect a small wobble when a new boundary appears in an old relationship. Wobbles settle. What rarely settles is the slow resentment of the boundary never set.

body.heading: Respecting theirs completes the circuit
paragraphs: The deal is reciprocal: the friend who goes quiet at nine, the colleague who needs the agenda in advance, the parent who will not discuss money at the table. Honouring boundaries you find inconvenient is the membership fee for having your own honoured.
In the long run, relationships with clear edges last longer than fused ones. Gardens need fences; so do people who intend to keep visiting each other for years.

takeaway: State boundaries early, as information about yourself — and honour other people’s the same way.
